description_full: Cushman & Wakefield Limited, together with its subsidiaries, provides commercial real estate services under the Cushman & Wakefield brand in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It offers integrated facilities management, project and development, portfolio administration, transaction management, and strategic consulting services; property management services, including client accounting, engineering and operations, lease compliance administration, project and development, tenant experience, residential property management, and sustainability services; self-performed facilities services, which include janitorial, maintenance, environment management, landscaping, and office services; and project management sustainability and workplace consulting services. The company also provides owner representation and tenant representation leasing services; debt and structured financing for real estate purchase and sales transactions; and appraisal management, investment management, valuation advisory, portfolio advisory, diligence advisory, dispute analysis and litigation support, financial reporting, and property and/or portfolio valuation services on real estate debt and equity decisions. It serves real estate owners and occupiers, such as tenants, investors, and multinational companies. The company was founded in 1784 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Cushman & Wakefield Ltd. is a mid-cap real estate business with a $3.1B market cap on $10.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $293M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.86× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 18pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.22x its revenue share).
It accounts for 2.9% of sector revenue and 0.6% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 27% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 1.31, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.75 vs 5y 1.48), so read it loosely.
About $29.4M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash and 55% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 54% below its DCF fair value of $28.95, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.75 to $38.41 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 9.4 vs 16.2 and P/FCF 10.7 vs 17.8, richer on P/E 45.9 vs 23.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 28% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $16.73 on average, 26% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.72).
It converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.86x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 3%.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.5x net debt to EBITDA ($784.2M of cash against $2.7B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.74 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.6% over 3 years and 5.6% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (0.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.4% on average.
Analysts expect 14.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $1.0M sold).
The share count has grown 1.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 53,000 employees, each generates about $194K of revenue, 0.1x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 2.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $6K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.8M (19x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
